title: John Nay — Norm Ai / Norm Law (agentic law and the AI-native full-service firm)
pub: AAA "AI and the Future of Law" (YouTube)
author: John Nay

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Nay confirms the operational premises that agents can perform first-pass work before human intervention and reduce reliance on associate teams, while barred attorneys retain supervision. But he redirects from the cluster’s expertise-reproduction and apprenticeship concern toward an AI-native delivery model built around persistent client-specific agents, partner judgment and outcome pricing; he does not propose deliberate training mechanisms for juniors.
qs: Those documents were analyzed by an agent behind the scenes before a human even stepped in at all.

That’s important because they can actually spend more time on that type of work than they could otherwise, because there are fewer teams and teams of associates to manage, and there is less work that they would necessarily need to be doing for the more traditional business development type work as well.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Nay accepts the value of client- and matter-specific context, but redirects the cluster’s predominantly verified-copilot framing toward preconfigured agents. He argues that persistent context removes repeated prompting and enables faster, parallel and more highly automated execution, though the supplied evidence does not address verification, reliability or professional accountability.
qs: Compared to a copilot, where you’d have to re-input that information in a way — you’d have to sort of implicitly train it again about that situation — that’s already been done, and that’s stable.
And it’s able to go further up the level of automation because of all that you’ve imbued into it ahead of time.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The excerpt contains only closing remarks expressing interest in AI-native firms and does not provide John Nay’s substantive views on whether lawyers should actively shape AI deployment, support implementation, or participate in governance.
qs: This has been super interesting, and I’m really excited to know more about AI-native firms.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Nay accepts the shift from copilot-style assistance to delegated, connected work and materially extends it in two ways: agents can retain matter-specific context and perform fuller first passes, while separate legal agents can govern other agents and make capabilities more amenable to benchmarking. His account supports bounded human intervention rather than lawyer-free practice, but offers proposed operating advantages rather than quantified reliability or net-benefit evidence.
qs: Whereas if it’s an AI agent, then you’re more likely to get that compounding benefit because the AI agent is doing more of the full pass of something.

But as the key systems are agentic — so think generating marketing, or talking directly to a client, or giving investment advice as an agent to a client — a lot of stuff that traditionally was human, that core economic activity, needs other AI agents to check that from a legal, regulatory, and compliance perspective.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Nay provides a concrete AI-native production model that integrates agentic first-pass work with attorney supervision, client partnership and value-oriented pricing. This materially develops the cluster’s institutional-absorption proposition, while remaining an operational account rather than measured evidence of productivity or broader transformation.
qs: Norm Law attorneys are supervising that work, and nothing goes out the door without that human supervision by a barred attorney who is doing that work for the client.

But then it’s also why we build big, long-term relationships with larger clients, because this allows us to really lean in and partner with them on, in some ways, co-developing the way to make sure that we are delivering the value and that the value is being priced correctly.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Nay accepts the cluster’s core proposition and supplies a concrete AI-native service model: agents automate bounded transactional and regulatory production, while barred attorneys supervise delivery and experienced lawyers concentrate on strategic judgment. Norm Law’s advance, outcome-oriented pricing and client-specific agents materially develop the cluster’s account of technology-enabled delivery, although the performance evidence remains company-reported and the model excludes highly unpredictable, bet-the-company work.
qs: Norm Law attorneys are supervising that work, and nothing goes out the door without that human supervision by a barred attorney who is doing that work for the client.
And then a lot of it also is the more traditional working with clients and providing strategic judgment, but not on the billable hour, and instead as part of a broader relationship with the client.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Nay supports the cluster’s view that legal AI requires service and organisational redesign rather than a standalone software purchase. He materially extends it with an AI-native delivery model combining lawyer–developer collaboration, attorney-supervised agents, long-term client co-development of value and pricing, and deliberate recruitment into AI-oriented roles.
qs: Norm Law attorneys are supervising that work, and nothing goes out the door without that human supervision by a barred attorney who is doing that work for the client.

But then it’s also why we build big, long-term relationships with larger clients, because this allows us to really lean in and partner with them on, in some ways, co-developing the way to make sure that we are delivering the value and that the value is being priced correctly.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Norm Law accepts the cluster’s core proposition and provides a concrete AI-native operating model for it: agents automate substantial work within bounded, predictable workflows, while barred attorneys supervise delivery and retain strategic judgment. Its workflow co-development and upfront unit pricing materially extend the synthesis by showing how selective deployment can reshape service delivery and incentives, though the evidence is primarily Nay’s account rather than independent validation.
qs: Norm Law attorneys are supervising that work, and nothing goes out the door without that human supervision by a barred attorney who is doing that work for the client.
We’re not going to be doing things where it’s very hard for both sides to understand ahead of time exactly what’s going to be entailed.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Nay directly supports the cluster’s core proposition: practical agentic legal work depends on sustained collaboration among legal experts, legal engineers and software engineers, plus persistent client-specific context. His first-pass automation model retains human involvement for strategic judgment. The account is operational but largely company-reported and does not establish broad reliability or show that tacit expertise transfers easily.
qs: All three are collaborating — especially the legal engineer and the partner — every single day to embed that knowledge that the partners have from decades of experience into these AI agents.

Then we come to the client, and we can embed, on top of that base AI agent that could apply to anybody, a client overlay of their precedent and their past deals or past contracts — whatever is the focus for that matter type.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: Nay supports the cluster’s core proposition by presenting an AI-native legal-delivery model in which barred attorneys supervise and sign off on work, making human accountability central to client trust. His recruitment comments also align with the cluster’s view that new delivery economics require organisational and staffing adaptation, though they do not resolve the wider apprenticeship or succession problem.
qs: Norm Law attorneys are supervising that work, and nothing goes out the door without that human supervision by a barred attorney who is doing that work for the client.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: Nay supports the cluster’s practitioner-led experimentation proposition by describing AI as a practical aid for developing research hypotheses and sustaining involvement in legal-AI research despite limited time. The excerpts provide experiential support for AI-assisted professional work, but no evidence about reliability, outcomes, implementation models or Norm Law’s agentic operations.
qs: We launched something recently called the Legal AGI Lab, and the only way that I can have time to get involved in that is to use AI to help with developing research hypotheses and thinking through ways to carry forward the work that we do there.
So it’s sort of like a meta AI legal AI, because it’s using AI to help research legal AI.

kp.k: Agentic law combines task automation with AI governance
kp.d: Nay defines agentic law as embedding law into AI agents. He presents two applications: automating first-pass legal and regulatory operations, and checking other agents' economic activities for legal, regulatory and compliance issues. His argument is that increasingly agentic systems require governance beyond the relatively deterministic guardrails used for earlier systems.
qs: So agentic law is embedding law into AI agents, to put it really simply.

So for us, building agentic law unlocks both sides of the coin: automating some of the first-pass work that happens in a more prosaic way, but then also unlocking the ability of AI to be deployed as agents.

kp.k: Agents promise compounding learning beyond copilot efficiency
kp.d: Nay argues that copilots improve immediate efficiency but generally fail to embed completed work into a reusable system with compounding benefits. By contrast, agents performing fuller processes can incorporate operational learning. He also argues that separating agent performance from human activity makes capabilities easier to benchmark and improve systematically. These are his comparative claims, not quantified findings presented in the transcript.
qs: When you use AI as a copilot, it’s definitely an efficiency booster.
Whereas if it’s an AI agent, then you’re more likely to get that compounding benefit because the AI agent is doing more of the full pass of something.

Whereas if you have an AI agent, then you can understand the jagged edge of capabilities — what it can and can’t do. And you can benchmark that, and you can systematically study that offline and online.

kp.k: Deal agents automate intake and background first-pass review
kp.d: In Nay's deal-review example, an agent analyzes incoming documents before a lawyer intervenes, using matter-specific knowledge and client preferences. He contrasts this with lawyers prompting copilots against forms, playbooks and term sheets. He claims agents can work asynchronously and in parallel, cover more issues and retain context across deals; the midnight-to-12:35 a.m. interval is illustrative rather than a reported performance measurement.
qs: So things came in the door. Those documents were analyzed by an agent behind the scenes before a human even stepped in at all.
The docs could have come in at midnight, and that was running from midnight to 12:35 a.m.
And it’s compounding, even, because as you do the next deal for that client, it had that previous deal for that agent for that client.

kp.k: Agent development combines legal engineers, technologists and practitioners
kp.d: Nay describes three collaborating roles: legal engineers, software and AI engineers, and practicing Norm Law attorneys. Most legal engineers arrive around fifth-year associate level with little coding experience and shift into full-time agent building, testing and deployment rather than legal practice. Technologists supply production infrastructure, while practicing lawyers, especially experienced partners, contribute substantive expertise.
qs: There are legal engineers. This is a career that we developed a couple years ago, where we bring in attorneys — most of them are around the fifth-year associate level from other law firms — and almost none of them have written a lot of code before they join.
So their day-to-day is building and refining and testing and deploying AI agents. That’s their full-time job. They’re not practicing law.
All three are collaborating — especially the legal engineer and the partner — every single day to embed that knowledge that the partners have from decades of experience into these AI agents.

kp.k: Client overlays retain knowledge beyond individual associate tenure
kp.d: Nay describes matter-specific base agents augmented with client precedents, contracts and past deals. These client overlays accumulate knowledge through subsequent work and remain associated with the client. He presents this as a continuity advantage over knowledge held by associates who may leave, rather than providing measured retention or service-quality evidence.
qs: Then we come to the client, and we can embed, on top of that base AI agent that could apply to anybody, a client overlay of their precedent and their past deals or past contracts — whatever is the focus for that matter type.
The agent overlay on the client level can get thicker and thicker as we move forward and do more and more work for the client.
now this digital associate is there, and it’s not going to leave.

kp.k: Upfront matter pricing replaces billable human hours
kp.d: Nay says Norm Law primarily prices by outcome, operationalized as an agreed advance price for a deal, agreement review or other unit of work, often informed by the client's historical spending. He argues this removes extra charges for additional availability and incentivizes the provider to improve speed and service through both technology and people. No fee amounts or realized savings are supplied.
qs: We don’t price by billable human hours.
We primarily price by outcome.
We align on a price ahead of time.
And then on our side, obviously, we are incentivized to really lean in as much as possible to improving the service for them and making it faster by using technology in addition to humans.

kp.k: Pricing uncertainty constrains matters and favors long-term clients
kp.d: Nay acknowledges that anticipating matter scope and compensating unpredictable work is difficult. Initially, the firm excludes work whose requirements neither side can understand sufficiently in advance. Its model instead favors larger clients and substantial long-term relationships, enabling collaborative pricing development and averaging across matters that require more or less work.
qs: We’re not going to be doing things where it’s very hard for both sides to understand ahead of time exactly what’s going to be entailed.
So it tilts us toward getting these long-term relationships with clients where we’re going to commit to doing a lot together.
And then that allows us to also average out between some things that maybe take longer or take less long.

kp.k: Autonomous first passes retain mandatory lawyer supervision
kp.d: In response to the host's question about work without humans in the loop, Nay distinguishes front-end building, testing and validation from supervision and final signoff. He states that no client work leaves without supervision by a barred attorney. Thus, his model automates initial processing without claiming unsupervised delivery of legal services. He names Blackstone and Coatue as clients and attributes their comfort to the supervising team; these are company-reported client claims.
qs: Norm Law attorneys are supervising that work, and nothing goes out the door without that human supervision by a barred attorney who is doing that work for the client.
So it has that final layer, that final supervision, and final signoff fully baked in on the top.
Blackstone is a client of ours, and so is Coatue.
They’ve gotten comfortable with the team that we have that is able to supervise the work and communicate it to them.

kp.k: Partner work shifts toward engineering collaboration and strategic judgment
kp.d: Nay describes partners collaborating directly with legal engineers on workflows while continuing client advice. He claims fewer associate teams to manage and less traditional business-development work preserve more partner time for strategic judgment. The transcript describes a changed allocation of partner work but supplies no staffing ratios or measured time savings.
qs: They might walk in here — we’re all here together in One World Trade Center — and sit down with a legal engineer and talk through certain workflows that they would like to be working on building together.
there are fewer teams and teams of associates to manage, and there is less work that they would necessarily need to be doing for the more traditional business development type work as well.
So it allows them to preserve more of their precious time for the strategic judgment that clients want out of the partner-level engagement.

kp.k: Recruitment targets experienced lawyers seeking a different operating model
kp.d: Nay acknowledges that the novel role complicates recruitment and requires self-selection. He says the attraction includes passing AI benefits to clients, escaping perceived incumbent business-model constraints and building reusable agents alongside engineers. As examples of recruitment, he names Mike Schmidtberger, Alan Weil, Justin Rattigan and Sam Lipson, drawing from senior law-firm and in-house positions; these examples support his account of hiring rather than a profession-wide labor-market finding.
qs: You just have to be clear about what the role is and allow people to self-select into it, because it’s definitely not for everybody.

And then the unique ability to collaborate with AI engineers and legal engineers every day, and be part of this project of building lasting value and building AI agents that understand law, is just a really fun project to work on.
many of them with decades of experience at traditional firms, at top firms, or in top in-house jobs

kp.k: Current practice focuses on financial-services transactions and regulation
kp.d: Although the host introduces Norm Law as the world's first AI-native full-service firm, Nay describes a narrower current agent focus: real estate transactions, finance and funds; private and registered funds; private equity; venture capital; emerging companies; and primarily SEC regulatory work. Clients are primarily New York financial-services firms. He expressly excludes a current focus on bet-the-company agent work.
qs: So it’s transactional work, funds work, and also regulatory work, primarily SEC regulatory.
primarily, right now, financial services firms here in New York.
In terms of what we’re not doing, we’re not focused on bet-the-company AI agents for bet-the-company work.

kp.k: Norm AI supplies technology; Norm Law delivers legal services
kp.d: Nay distinguishes the technology company, which serves in-house teams directly through software and develops the agents, from the affiliated law firm, whose attorneys practice law for clients. Norm AI also powers much of Norm Law's behind-the-scenes work. The transcript does not describe ownership arrangements or identify professional-rule permissions for this affiliation.
qs: Norm AI is a technology company, and we serve in-house teams directly. When I say directly, I mean through technology.
And then Norm AI powers much of the affiliated law firm, Norm Law, in its AI agents behind the scenes.
And then Norm Law is the law firm that is serving the client. So the attorneys who are practicing law are practicing law at Norm Law.

kp.k: Legal AGI Lab develops use-specific proprietary benchmarks
kp.d: Nay describes the lab's automation research as applied benchmarking to identify what AI can reliably perform in specific high-stakes legal and regulatory settings. This combines AI engineering and research with lawyers' use-case knowledge. No benchmark names, sample sizes, scores or measured reliability results are reported.
qs: a lot of that is around proprietary benchmarking work — building out applied benchmarks to really understand, in high-stakes, specific scenarios, what AI can and can’t do, and where you can really trust it to do certain work.
That part is very AI engineering and AI research focused, but with a strong overlay of lawyer understanding in specific use cases.

kp.k: Governance research examines agent intentionality and fiduciary standards
kp.d: Nay presents law as a democratically determined basis for AI alignment and describes research into how nonhuman agents could fit within legal rules. Topics include contractual and criminal intentionality and fiduciary standards for AI investment advice. He reports a paper posted on Stanford Law School's website, co-authored with a Vanderbilt professor, alongside simulations and tests informed by securities lawyers and former regulators. These are research questions and activities, not reported conclusions that agents possess legal intent or fiduciary status.
qs: using law as a democratically determined database of what AI should and shouldn’t do — for a form of AI alignment, is one way to think about it.
So how much intention did an AI agent have? How do you measure that? And how do you see if it passes a test that a human would be put through in the legal analysis?
we run a bunch of simulations, see how AI agents would respond, and see if they pass different tests for intentionality.
We’re also doing a lot of work around fiduciary duties and how well AI agents could be subject to those types of rules and standards.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Nay claims that agentic law enables both first-pass legal automation and legal/compliance oversight of other AI agents.
pts.d: John Nay defines agentic law as embedding law into AI agents. He argues that increasingly agentic economic activities, including marketing, client communications and investment advice, need other agents to check compliance. This is a proposed broader governance function as well as an account of his company's legal-operations approach.

pts.k: Nay claims that agents provide more reusable, compounding improvements and more identifiable capability boundaries than copilots.
pts.d: Nay describes copilots as efficiency-enhancing but says their work does not as naturally become a reusable operational asset. Agents performing fuller processes can incorporate operational learning and be benchmarked separately from human work. He presents this separation as enabling more informed delegation and targeted capability improvement, not as eliminating human verification.

pts.k: Nay claims that preconfigured transaction agents accelerate first-pass review and retain client-specific knowledge across matters.
pts.d: In Nay's deal-review example, an agent analyzes incoming documents before a human begins, using matter-type expertise and client preferences embedded beforehand. He says this permits background and parallel processing, broader review and greater automation. Client overlays incorporate precedents and previous matters, accumulating knowledge that, unlike an associate's personal knowledge, does not leave when an employee departs.

pts.k: Nay describes an AI-enabled pricing model that replaces human-hour billing with advance prices for defined work and rewards efficiency.
pts.d: Nay says Norm Law primarily prices by outcome, operationalized as an agreed price for a deal, agreement review or other unit of work, often informed by historical client spending. He argues this makes greater availability cost-neutral for clients and incentivizes technology-driven improvement. He also says pricing uncertainty narrows the initial matter selection and favors long-term relationships with larger clients, across which effort can be averaged.

pts.k: Nay claims that AI-native delivery changes legal roles and partner time allocation while retaining attorney accountability.
pts.d: Nay describes experienced associates moving into full-time legal-engineering roles building agents rather than practicing law, alongside software/AI engineers and practicing Norm Law lawyers. Partners help encode expertise and deliver strategic advice. He says fewer associate teams to manage and less traditional business-development work leave partners more time for judgment. Autonomous first-pass work remains subject to licensed-attorney supervision and final signoff; this is not direct, unsupervised reliance on agent output.

pts.k: Nay says client trust and senior-lawyer recruitment are achievable through human supervision and an innovation-aligned business model.
pts.d: Nay attributes client comfort to the lawyers supervising and communicating the work. He describes recruitment as more complicated but feasible through self-selection by lawyers interested in passing AI benefits to clients and building lasting systems. He claims traditional firms' business models and lack of innovation can prevent those benefits from being passed through.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The operational and commercial claims rest principally on Nay's first-person account, examples and named clients and hires.
pts.d: Nay offers experience from building and operating Norm AI/Norm Law rather than quantitative comparative findings. His midnight-to-12:35 deal-review scenario is illustrative, not a reported timing study. He names Blackstone and Coatue as clients and points to website testimonials, without reproducing them. Named senior recruits include Mike Schmidtberger, Alan Weil, Justin Rattigan and Sam Lipson. The interview supplies no measured accuracy, cost savings, productivity gains, retention rates or recruiting statistics.

pts.k: Nay describes proprietary benchmarking and legal/technical research, but reports no benchmark scores or research results.
pts.d: The Legal AGI Lab's stated work includes applied benchmarks for specific high-stakes tasks, agent simulations and intentionality tests, and fiduciary-duty research with securities-lawyer and former-regulator oversight. Nay cites a paper posted on Stanford Law School's website and coauthored with a Vanderbilt law professor. These establish the research activities he invokes, not demonstrated results about agent reliability, legal intention or fiduciary compliance.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Nay presents the delivery model as current at the interview, with restricted workflows, substantial advance preparation and continuing human supervision.
pts.d: In the interview labeled 2026, Nay identifies current agent development in real-estate transactions/finance/funds, private and registered funds, private equity, venture capital, emerging companies and primarily SEC regulatory work. He excludes current focus on bet-the-company agents and initially avoids work whose scope is difficult for both sides to predict. Claimed compounding benefits depend on prior engineering, partner expertise, client information and repeated matters. He gives no date for broader automation or general legal capability.

pts.k: The broader governance claims are conditional on growing agentic economic activity and remain an open research agenda.
pts.d: Nay says legal analysis will become important as agents undertake activities such as contracting or investment advice. Questions about intentionality, criminal activity and fiduciary standards are presented as matters to investigate, not settled conclusions that agents already possess legal intention or can independently meet fiduciary duties. No deployment timetable is provided.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate beneficiaries and affected roles are enterprise clients, in-house teams, experienced lawyers and engineers; the broader governance agenda reaches financial-services users and society.
pts.d: Nay's commercial account concerns large corporate clients, especially New York financial-services firms, rather than unmet civil legal need. Clients receive proposed faster service, advance pricing and persistent institutional knowledge. In-house teams buy technology from Norm AI, while Norm Law delivers legal services. Approximately fifth-year associates may transition into non-practicing legal-engineering roles; partners supervise agents, develop workflows and provide strategic judgment. Nay does not quantify associate displacement or predict a profession-wide staffing shape. His governance research also concerns investment advisers, recipients of AI-driven advice and the public affected by autonomous economic activity.
